title: Biodiversity Solutions and Tradeoffs Core Test
description: Core practice for evaluate human-impact solutions using biodiversity data, constraints, tradeoffs, and evidence-based design reasoning.

questions.prompt: What should an evidence-based biodiversity solution include?
questions.questionText: What should an evidence-based biodiversity solution include?
options: data about the problem and data to check whether the solution helps
only a drawing with no measurements
questions.correctAnswer: data about the problem and data to check whether the solution helps
questions.explanation: Solutions need evidence before and after.

questions.prompt: A town compares two wetland path designs. Which evidence matters most for biodiversity?
questions.questionText: A town compares two wetland path designs. Which evidence matters most for biodiversity?
options: how each path affects nesting areas and species counts
questions.correctAnswer: how each path affects nesting areas and species counts
questions.explanation: Biodiversity evidence should connect to organisms and habitat.

questions.prompt: Why do engineers consider constraints?
questions.questionText: Why do engineers consider constraints?
options: Constraints prove no solution can help.
Real solutions must work within limits like cost, safety, time, and space.
questions.correctAnswer: Real solutions must work within limits like cost, safety, time, and space.
questions.explanation: Constraints are real design limits.

questions.prompt: A plan protects more habitat but costs more. What concept does this show?
questions.questionText: A plan protects more habitat but costs more. What concept does this show?
questions.correctAnswer: a tradeoff
questions.explanation: A tradeoff means gaining one benefit while accepting a cost or limitation.

questions.prompt: Which model best fits solution design?
questions.questionText: Which model best fits solution design?
options: impact data -> goal -> solution options -> tradeoff comparison -> monitoring
questions.correctAnswer: impact data -> goal -> solution options -> tradeoff comparison -> monitoring
questions.explanation: The model follows evidence-based design.

questions.prompt: A park installs native plants to support pollinators. Which data would best test success?
questions.questionText: A park installs native plants to support pollinators. Which data would best test success?
options: number of letters on the sign
pollinator counts before and after planting
questions.correctAnswer: pollinator counts before and after planting
questions.explanation: Before-and-after counts can test the design.

questions.prompt: A student says, "The cheapest plan is automatically best." What is the best correction?
questions.questionText: A student says, "The cheapest plan is automatically best." What is the best correction?
options: The most expensive plan always wins.
Cost is one constraint, but effectiveness and ecosystem impact also matter.
questions.correctAnswer: Cost is one constraint, but effectiveness and ecosystem impact also matter.
questions.explanation: A best design balances evidence and constraints.

questions.prompt: Which claim is strongest?
questions.questionText: Which claim is strongest?
options: Plan B is better because it preserves 80% more nesting habitat while staying within the budget.
Plan B is better because I like it.
Plan A is better because its name is short.
questions.correctAnswer: Plan B is better because it preserves 80% more nesting habitat while staying within the budget.
questions.explanation: The strong claim uses data and a constraint.

questions.prompt: A solution reduces pesticide use but requires more hand-weeding. What should the team discuss?
questions.questionText: A solution reduces pesticide use but requires more hand-weeding. What should the team discuss?
options: whether the biodiversity benefit is worth the labor tradeoff
whether genes are sections of DNA
questions.correctAnswer: whether the biodiversity benefit is worth the labor tradeoff
questions.explanation: The team should compare benefit and cost.

questions.prompt: Which observation would show possible biodiversity decline?
questions.questionText: Which observation would show possible biodiversity decline?
options: the same trail map is used twice
the weather changes for one afternoon
fewer different species recorded in the same habitat over several years
questions.correctAnswer: fewer different species recorded in the same habitat over several years
questions.explanation: Species richness over time is biodiversity evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is monitoring important after a solution is built?
questions.questionText: Why is monitoring important after a solution is built?
options: It proves every solution is perfect.
It only makes the project longer.
It shows whether the solution actually changes the outcome.
It replaces the need for a problem.
questions.correctAnswer: It shows whether the solution actually changes the outcome.
questions.explanation: Monitoring connects design to results.

questions.prompt: A wildlife crossing is proposed over a road. Which evidence best supports the need?
questions.questionText: A wildlife crossing is proposed over a road. Which evidence best supports the need?
options: the number of cones in a photo
animal movement data showing the road blocks habitat connections
questions.correctAnswer: animal movement data showing the road blocks habitat connections
questions.explanation: Need evidence should match the problem.

questions.prompt: Which design goal is clearest?
questions.questionText: Which design goal is clearest?
options: Increase native plant cover by 30% in one year to support pollinators.
questions.correctAnswer: Increase native plant cover by 30% in one year to support pollinators.
questions.explanation: Clear goals are measurable.

questions.prompt: A solution helps one species but reduces habitat for another. What should happen next?
questions.questionText: A solution helps one species but reduces habitat for another. What should happen next?
options: Compare the impacts and revise the design if needed.
questions.correctAnswer: Compare the impacts and revise the design if needed.
questions.explanation: Tradeoffs should lead to evaluation and revision.

questions.prompt: Which data table would be most useful?
questions.questionText: Which data table would be most useful?
options: alphabetical list of plant names only
species counts, habitat area protected, cost, and maintenance needs for each plan
questions.correctAnswer: species counts, habitat area protected, cost, and maintenance needs for each plan
questions.explanation: A useful table compares benefits and constraints.

questions.prompt: Why does biodiversity matter for ecosystem stability?
questions.questionText: Why does biodiversity matter for ecosystem stability?
options: More variety can help ecosystems continue functioning when conditions change.
Biodiversity means every organism is identical.
questions.correctAnswer: More variety can help ecosystems continue functioning when conditions change.
questions.explanation: Variety can support resilience, though it is not magic.

questions.prompt: A school replaces lawn with native plants. Which result best supports success?
questions.questionText: A school replaces lawn with native plants. Which result best supports success?
options: more native pollinator visits and lower water use after installation
the garden has a longer nickname
questions.correctAnswer: more native pollinator visits and lower water use after installation
questions.explanation: This combines biodiversity and constraint data.

questions.prompt: Which statement avoids the perfect-solution trap?
questions.questionText: Which statement avoids the perfect-solution trap?
options: A design must solve every problem completely.
Evidence is optional if the idea sounds kind.
A design can be worth using if evidence shows improvement and tradeoffs are acceptable.
questions.correctAnswer: A design can be worth using if evidence shows improvement and tradeoffs are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Engineering often improves outcomes within limits.

questions.prompt: A creek restoration plan removes invasive plants but may disturb soil for a week. What question is best?
questions.questionText: A creek restoration plan removes invasive plants but may disturb soil for a week. What question is best?
options: Does the creek have a short name?
Are all plants equally helpful everywhere?
Will long-term habitat gains outweigh short-term disturbance?
questions.correctAnswer: Will long-term habitat gains outweigh short-term disturbance?
questions.explanation: The question weighs tradeoffs over time.

questions.prompt: Which cause/effect chain is strongest?
questions.questionText: Which cause/effect chain is strongest?
options: less habitat fragmentation -> easier movement -> more connected populations
more signs -> more fossils -> more DNA
questions.correctAnswer: less habitat fragmentation -> easier movement -> more connected populations
questions.explanation: Connected habitat can support movement and populations.

questions.prompt: A plan is popular but data shows no increase in species richness after two years. What should the team do?
questions.questionText: A plan is popular but data shows no increase in species richness after two years. What should the team do?
options: revise the plan using the monitoring evidence
keep it unchanged because popularity is enough
questions.correctAnswer: revise the plan using the monitoring evidence
questions.explanation: Monitoring data should guide revision.

questions.prompt: Which solution is most targeted?
questions.questionText: Which solution is most targeted?
options: install shaded streamside plants where temperature data shows overheating
questions.correctAnswer: install shaded streamside plants where temperature data shows overheating
questions.explanation: Targeted solutions match evidence to cause.

questions.prompt: Why compare multiple solutions?
questions.questionText: Why compare multiple solutions?
options: Different designs can meet the same goal with different benefits and tradeoffs.
Only the first idea can work.
questions.correctAnswer: Different designs can meet the same goal with different benefits and tradeoffs.
questions.explanation: Comparison supports stronger design choices.

questions.prompt: A bird nesting area is declining near a trail. Which design change best fits the evidence?
questions.questionText: A bird nesting area is declining near a trail. Which design change best fits the evidence?
options: remove all signs about the area
reroute the trail away from nesting habitat during sensitive seasons
questions.correctAnswer: reroute the trail away from nesting habitat during sensitive seasons
questions.explanation: Reducing disturbance near nests matches the problem.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would weaken a claimed solution?
questions.questionText: Which evidence would weaken a claimed solution?
options: species counts continue falling after the solution and no other data shows improvement
water use decreased while pollinators increased
questions.correctAnswer: species counts continue falling after the solution and no other data shows improvement
questions.explanation: A solution claim needs outcome evidence.

questions.prompt: A team chooses a moderate-cost plan because it protects much more habitat than the cheap plan and is safer than the expensive plan. What reasoning is this?
questions.questionText: A team chooses a moderate-cost plan because it protects much more habitat than the cheap plan and is safer than the expensive plan. What reasoning is this?
questions.correctAnswer: balancing evidence, constraints, and tradeoffs
questions.explanation: The team compares multiple criteria.

questions.prompt: Which question pushes deeper thinking?
questions.questionText: Which question pushes deeper thinking?
options: Can the plan be named quickly?
What evidence would convince us the solution helped biodiversity without creating a worse tradeoff?
questions.correctAnswer: What evidence would convince us the solution helped biodiversity without creating a worse tradeoff?
questions.explanation: It asks for evidence and tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: Why should a solution name the organisms affected?
questions.questionText: Why should a solution name the organisms affected?
options: Different organisms may respond differently, so the evidence must be specific.
All organisms always respond the same way.
questions.correctAnswer: Different organisms may respond differently, so the evidence must be specific.
questions.explanation: Specific affected groups make claims testable.

questions.prompt: Which final explanation shows strong understanding?
questions.questionText: Which final explanation shows strong understanding?
options: The best biodiversity solution is supported by data, meets the goal, and manages constraints and tradeoffs.
The best solution is whichever sounds kind.
Any solution with a tradeoff fails.
questions.correctAnswer: The best biodiversity solution is supported by data, meets the goal, and manages constraints and tradeoffs.
questions.explanation: This captures evidence-based design.

questions.prompt: Which investigation would improve a wetland plan?
questions.questionText: Which investigation would improve a wetland plan?
options: Ask only which path is shortest
Measure species counts, nesting success, path safety, and cost for each design option.
questions.correctAnswer: Measure species counts, nesting success, path safety, and cost for each design option.
questions.explanation: Good investigations compare ecological outcomes and constraints.
